pages.text: CodentGIS's Diary | Project in the Mud | OpenStreetMap Select Language Loading... Close CodentGIS's Diary Project in the Mud Posted by CodentGIS on 17 August 2026 in English . Oh, where do I start? It was around October when I had recently imported the barangay boundaries of my hometown, Cauayan City. I had just asked the GIS team at the local Planning and Development Office to adjust the boundaries again, as many issues were identified in the dataset. A while later, I had an idea to try to help the GIS team adjust the boundaries, because I figured, “Why not?” and they’re probably doing a lot of work already, given so many developments in the area. A little back and forth, but then they stopped responding. I mean, it is basically a 50/50 chance that they respond or not. A little later, I dove into further research and stuff, and I thought of asking an institution to collaborate with me on making a dataset for the PDO to use and merge with theirs, so it can be as accurate as possible (I like things accurate). Thus, Project Cadastral Cauayan (CaCau) was born. I first emailed the Isabela State University. I chose them especially because of the Cauayan Campus. In my eyes, they were the most capable (and probably only) institution in the area to pull this off. It was February 27 of this year. No response, so I kept trying new email addresses, follow-ups, and at one point, Messenger. Too many alternatives with no response, and about two months later, nothing. Until finally, through the Cauayan Campus’ newspaper email, the Kawayan Communicator, a Messenger notification popped up.

pages.text: Colchester Army medics practise warzone rescue operation Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Weather Newsletters Army medics practise warzone rescue operation 7 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Leigh Milner , in Colchester and Henry Godfrey-Evans Leigh Milner/BBC Twenty medics took part in the exercise at Colchester Soldiers in Essex have been practising their ability to extract seriously injured casualties from the battlefield. The training exercise, involving the British Army's 16 Medical Regiment and the Royal Air Force's (RAF) Tactical Medical Wing, got under way at the Merville Barracks in Colchester on Tuesday. About 20 medics simulated a warzone scenario, where they might have to treat patients and rush them to a UK hospital. "Being able to patch soldiers up and get them back into the fight if deployed on large-scale combat operations is key," said Maj Ed Tusting, who commands a squadron with the 16 Medical Regiment. In a real scenario, the Army's light surgical teams would parachute into the warzone. For this exercise, medics patched up serious wounds on model patients - including a life-size dummy - in a pitched tent at the barracks. Once stabilised, personnel were driven to a helicopter where they were airlifted to RAF Honington in Suffolk. Next, the team boarded an A400M plane and were flown in circles above the RAF base to mimic what would otherwise have been a journey to a UK hospital. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Colorado State Office The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) manages more than 8.3 million acres of public lands and more than 27 million acres of mineral estate in Colorado - mostly concentrated in the western part of the state. BLM lands in Colorado range from alpine tundra, colorful canyons and mesas in the southwest, to rolling sage covered hills in the northwest. The public owns more than one-third of Colorado. BLM Colorado adheres to multiple-use management, managing public lands for both commercial and public uses based on sound science. The economic health of many Colorado communities is supported by ranching, energy development and tourism associated with public lands. Public lands offer recreational opportunities, cultural resources, resource and energy potential, and vast open spaces. Colorado’s lands produce vast amounts of coal, oil, natural gas and geothermal power to help meet the nation’s energy needs. Congenital Zika Syndrome and Other Birth Defects For Everyone Oct. 26, 2026 What to know Zika virus can spread from an infected pregnant woman to her fetus. Infection during pregnancy can lead to congenital Zika syndrome and other birth defects. Zika virus infection does not impact future pregnancies. Overview of Zika-associated birth defects Zika virus infection during pregnancy can cause birth defects of the brain or eye. These birth defects can occur alone or with developmental problems in a particular pattern called congenital Zika syndrome. The following conditions can occur in a baby with congenital Zika virus infection: Smaller than expected head size, called microcephaly Problems with brain development Feeding problems, such as difficulty swallowing Hearing loss and vision problems Seizures Decreased joint movement, called contractures Stiff muscles, making it difficult to move Not all babies born with congenital Zika syndrome will have all of these conditions. Video by Nicely Done Productions By Sam Kent Last updated August 12, 2026 Cities are constantly evolving. They are built up, layer by layer, each generation leaving its mark on the one before. Roman roads became the foundation for medieval streets. Aqueducts gave way to railways, electricity, and underground transportation. Over time, every city’s infrastructure becomes a record of the people who shaped it years before. Walk through Rome, and the history is impossible to ignore. Ancient walls sit beside modern apartments; the remains of a long-gone empire lie under busy streets. Layers of the past can be felt everywhere: yet Rome, just like every great city, cannot stand still. Today, millions of visitors and residents move through the city, expecting to stay connected above and below ground. From GPS and wayfinding tools to digital tickets and tap-to-pay features for transport systems, to instant communication between families and friends.
